- **Undeclared dependencies.** `nitropack` v2 put its own dependencies into the server bundle, so a file could import something like `lru-cache` without depending on it and still work. Add the package to your own dependencies, or report it to the module that needs it.

-- **Types.** If you augment `nitropack/types`, update it to the new module paths. See [Route Rule Types Move to `h3/rules`](#route-rule-types-move-to-h3rules). The layer changes how your server code runs, not how it type-checks. `useRuntimeConfig(event)` in a server route is still reported, because typed `$fetch` responses check route files alongside your app code, and an `H3Event` imported from a project dependency on h3 v1 does not match Nitro v3's event.

+- **Types.** The layer mostly changes how your server code runs, not how it type-checks. With `nitroLegacy.specifiers`, an augmentation of `nitropack` or `nitropack/types`, in your code or a module's, applies to the Nitro v3 interface of the same name, such as `NitroRuntimeHooks`. Augmentations of `nitropack/runtime` and `#internal/nitro` are not picked up, and route rules are declared elsewhere (see [Route Rule Types Move to `h3/rules`](#route-rule-types-move-to-h3rules)). With `nitroLegacy.h3`, `h3` resolves to Nitro's h3 v2 in the server tsconfig, even if your project depends on h3 v1, so an `H3Event` imported from `h3` matches the event your handlers receive. On that type, `event.node` is optional. Helpers that only h3 v1 has, such as `send`, `sendError` or `isStream`, still work when imported from `h3`, but they don't type-check that way. Their auto-imports are typed. `useRuntimeConfig(event)` in a server route is still reported, because typed `$fetch` responses check route files alongside your app code. For the same reason, an `H3Event` from `h3` in a server route is still reported by the app tsconfig, which resolves `h3` to your project's dependency.

- **The event object.** With the default builder, `event` is h3 v2's event. The layer adds back some things h3 v2 dropped, such as `event.context.nitro`, `event.context._nitro.routeRules` and a Node-shaped `event.node` on runtimes that don't have one. Requests made in process, such as a server-side `$fetch` or `useFetch` to one of your own routes or a page being prerendered, get one too, with an `event.node.req.socket` whose `readyState` is `'readOnly'`, as in Nitro v2. Its `remoteAddress` is the client address of the request that made the call, or `undefined` when there is none. Headers and the status you set on `event.node.res` apply to the response that Nitro sends.

- **The `close` hook while prerendering.** Nitro v3 stops the prerenderer without calling the runtime `close` hook, so a listener that saves data there never runs, and the data is lost. Nuxt names each Nitro v2 plugin that registers one with `NUXT_E8017`. Save the data as each route is prerendered instead, and read it back in a build hook.
